Text:
Each Arabic long vowel has one short vowel that matches it:

alif (aa) — {{c1::fatHa}}

waaw (uu) — {{c1::Damma}}

yaa (ii) — {{c1::kasra}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the long vowel is a whole LETTER you write on the line; its short partner is only a mark added above or below.

Distinguish: same vowel, two lengths — the long one is a letter you write, the short one a mark you add last.
verified_against: the marked sentence(s) on rendered p52 (printed 34), p53 (printed 35)
verified_by: read off the page render at 200 dpi (the scan's Arabic OCR is unreliable)

Text: An Arabic long vowel is held {{c1::at least twice}} as long as a short one — and English has {{c2::no long vowels at all}}, so Arabic's should feel exaggerated to you.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: do not worry about holding one "too long" — stretch it out so you can hear the difference.

Why: vowel length changes meaning, and a mispronounced length can make the word unintelligible.
verified_against: the marked sentence(s) on rendered p47 (printed 29), p52 (printed 34)
verified_by: read off the page render at 200 dpi (the scan's Arabic OCR is unreliable)

Text: Of Arabic's three long vowels, waaw is the {{c1::second::first / second / third}}, and its sound is that of {{c2::the exclamation of delight — ooooo!}}
Back Extra:
Cue: it shares its shape with the short vowel Damma, which is written as a miniature waaw.

Cue: your Unit 1 card teaches the same vowel as oo in poodle.

Pitfall: do not confuse it with English o or u; keep the mouth rounded and hold it.

Text: The last of Arabic's three long vowels is yaa, the sound of {{c1::ee in beep}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: imitate a honking car horn — beeeeep! — and exaggerate it to feel the length.

Cue: your Unit 1 card teaches the same vowel as ie in piece.

Ex: the book's own practice words are beep and street.
verified_against: the marked sentence(s) on rendered p49 (printed 31)
verified_by: read off the page render at 200 dpi (the scan's Arabic OCR is unreliable)

Text: A short vowel is written on the letter that {{c1::precedes}} it, never on one that follows.
Back Extra:
Why: an Arabic syllable always BEGINS with a consonant, so the mark rides on that consonant — the first letter of its syllable.

Cue: writing the vowels is the third and final step — skeleton first, then the dots, then the vowels.

Pitfall: in ordinary text the short vowels are usually not written at all.

Text: What decides how frontal or how deep a short vowel actually sounds is {{c1::the consonants surrounding it}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: fatHa runs from e in bet to u in but; kasra from ee in keep to i in bit.

Cue: each short vowel swings along the same axis its long partner does.

Text: At its most frontal, fatHa is {{c1::e as in bet}}; when deep, it is {{c1::u as in but}}.
Back Extra:
Why: it swings along the same frontal-to-deep axis its long counterpart alif does, and the consonants around it decide where it lands.

Pitfall: alif and fatHa do NOT share keywords — alif's deep pole is the long a of father, fatHa's is the short u of but. Same colour, different length.

Text: Of the consonants Unit 2 teaches, the frontal ones — the ones that pull a neighbouring short vowel toward the front of the mouth — are {{c1::baa, taa and thaa}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: all three share one skeleton and differ only in their dots — and all three are frontal.

Pitfall: the book names these as EXAMPLES of frontal consonants, not as the complete set — Arabic also has deep (emphatic) consonants, which pull the same vowel the other way.

Text: fatHa is written as {{c1::a short, slanted line segment}} {{c2::above::above or below?}} its consonant.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Damma sits in the same place, above the letter, but is shaped like a miniature waaw.

Cue: the vowel marks go on last — consonant skeleton first, then the dots, then the vowels.

Text: The name of the short vowel fatHa means {{c1::"opening"}}.
Back Extra:
Why: it names the shape of your mouth as you say it — wide open. Try it and see.

Distinguish: Damma is named for ROUNDING the mouth, not for opening it.

Text: After frontal consonants, Damma is pronounced {{c1::oo as in booth}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: English u in but and gum is a deep fatHa, NOT a Damma.

Cue: your Unit 1 card teaches this same vowel as oo in poodle — one sound, two keywords.

Cue: the name Damma refers to ROUNDING — keep your mouth rounded and it comes out right.

Why: a deep consonant pulls it deeper, closer to oo in wool.

Text: kasra ranges from a frontal {{c1::ee as in keep}} to a deep {{c1::i as in bit}}.
Back Extra: Why: as with fatHa and Damma, the surrounding consonants decide the exact sound.
verified_against: the marked sentence(s) on rendered p55 (printed 37)

Text: The name kasra means {{c1::"break"}}, and it refers to your mouth being {{c1::only slightly open}} as you say it.
Back Extra:
Cue: the name describes the MOUTH, not the sound — slightly open, not wide open.

Pitfall: do not drop the jaw for it; that turns it into a different vowel.

Text: English spells two distinct sounds th, and Arabic gives each its own letter. thaa is {{c1::only the three sound, never the that sound}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: thaa carries THREE dots — say "three" out loud before you pronounce or read it.

Distinguish: the th of that belongs to dhaal, a letter this course has not taught yet — Unit 1 drilled hearing the two apart.

Text: In social as well as professional situations it is polite to {{c1::shake hands}} when meeting or greeting another person of {{c2::the same gender::same or opposite?}}.
Back Extra: Why: with the opposite gender it varies widely according to religious belief and personal practice.

Back Extra: Why: her offered hand is the signal that she wants to shake yours.

Text:
‎{{c1::برافو}}

Transliteration: {{c1::braafoo}}

{{c2::Bravo!}} — said on finishing the first four letters of the alphabet
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — a borrowed exclamation of praise, written in Arabic letters.

Ex: "Bravo! You have learned the first four letters of the Arabic alphabet."

Distinguish: aHsanta is her spoken "Good job! Well done!"; this one is specifically Bravo!, and it is the book's word, not hers.

verified_by: external-anchor warning CLEARED: lexicon.py's in_source hit for 'conson' is a fragment of footnote 2 on p52 ('...consonant-short vowel)') — an occurrence of the word, not a definition, so there is nothing for the authored answer to agree with. The book never defines the term.
Text: A consonant is {{c1::a sound that blocks or narrows the airflow}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "syllables in Arabic always begin with a consonant."

Distinguish: a vowel is the open, freely flowing sound; a consonant closes or narrows it.

Cue: in Arabic the consonants are the skeleton you write first; the vowels are added last.

verified_by: external-anchor warning CLEARED: the in_source hit for 'short_vowel' is p52's long/short CORRESPONDENCE sentence (aa-fatHa, uu-Damma, ii-kasra). It never mentions length, so it cannot confirm a length-based definition.
Text: A short vowel is {{c1::as long as an ordinary English vowel}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "by convention, short vowels are written above or below the consonant."

Distinguish: in Arabic a short vowel is a MARK added above or below a consonant; a long vowel is a whole letter standing on the line.

Pitfall: they are usually left unwritten altogether, which is why reading unvowelled Arabic is a separate skill.

Text: A syllable is {{c1::one beat of a word}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "syllables in Arabic always begin with a consonant."

Meaning: one beat — a vowel plus the consonants packed around it.

Cue: a syllable holding a long vowel is almost always the stressed one.

Distinguish: a syllable is heard; a letter is written.
